segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul, called to be an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, and Sosthenes our brother,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to the assembly of God that is in Corinth, to those made holy in Christ Jesus, called to be holy ones, together with all those who in every place call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, their Lord and ours:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I always thank my God for you because of the grace of God that was given to you in Christ Jesus,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for in everything you were made rich in him, in all speech and all knowledge,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: just as the testimony about Christ was established among you,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that you are not lacking in any gift as you eagerly await the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He will also establish you to the end, beyond reproach on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: God is faithful, and through him you were called into partnership with his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now I appeal to you, brothers and sisters, through the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be knit together in the same mind and the same judgment.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it has been made clear to me about you, my brothers and sisters, by Chloe’s people, that there are quarrels among you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What I mean is this: each of you is saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I belong to Paul,” “I belong to Apollos,” “I belong to Cephas,” “I belong to Christ.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Has Christ been divided up? Paul was not crucified for you, was he? Or were you baptized into the name of Paul?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I am thankful that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that no one can say that you were baptized into my name.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I did also baptize the household of Stephanas; beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Christ did not send me to baptize but to proclaim the good news, and not with wisdom of words, so that the cross of Christ would not be made empty.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the intelligence of the intelligent I will set aside.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Where is the wise person? Where is the scholar? Where is the debater of this age? Has God not made the wisdom of the world foolish?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not come to know God through wisdom, God was pleased, through the foolishness of the proclamation, to save those who believe.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Jews ask for signs and Greeks seek wisdom,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but we proclaim Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the foolishness of God is wiser than human beings, and the weakness of God is stronger than human beings.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Look at your own calling, brothers and sisters: not many were wise by human standards, not many were powerful, not many were well-born.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise, and God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and God chose the low-born things of the world and the despised, the things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that no flesh may boast before God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It is from him that you are in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and holiness and redemption,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that, as it is written,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.”

notes.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering of citizens, and in the Greek Old Testament it names Israel assembled before God. ‘Church’ is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. ‘Assembly’ is used throughout this translation so that the reader sees one Greek word, though it can wrongly sound like a one-off meeting.

Paul uses this term for all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Greek Old Testament’s language for Israel. ‘Saints’ now suggests canonised individuals or people of unusual virtue. Many translations keep ‘saints’; others use ‘God’s people’. The preceding ‘made holy’ is the related verb.

The Greek says only ‘theirs and ours’, which could go with ‘Lord’ (he is Lord of believers everywhere as well as of Paul and the Corinthians) or with ‘place’ (‘in every place, theirs and ours’). Most translations and commentators take it with ‘Lord’, as here, but the word order allows the other reading.

The word means sharing something in common and was used of business partnerships, marriage and other joint ventures. ‘Fellowship’ is the traditional rendering but now tends to suggest friendly socialising. The Greek phrase could also be read as ‘sharing in his Son’, that is, participation in Christ and not only association with him; the two readings are not far apart.

notes.traditional: those of the household of Chloe
notes.note: The Greek says simply ‘those of Chloe’, meaning members of her household, most likely slaves, freed persons or business agents who travelled between Corinth and Ephesus, where Paul was writing. Nothing else is known about Chloe, including whether she lived in Corinth or was herself a believer.

Cephas is the Aramaic name, meaning ‘rock’, of the apostle better known by its Greek equivalent, Peter. Paul usually calls him Cephas. Whether Peter had actually visited Corinth or was simply revered there by some is not known.
Some of the earliest manuscripts read simply ‘I give thanks’, which is the text translated here. Most manuscripts add ‘to God’, and many English versions follow them. The sense is hardly affected.

Trained public speaking was highly prized in Greek cities such as Corinth, and a speaker’s skill was taken as a sign of his wisdom and standing. Paul’s phrase, literally ‘wisdom of word’, refers to that kind of polished rhetoric or clever argument. The same Greek term is picked up in the next verse as ‘the word of the cross’, so ‘word’ is kept in both places.

notes.phrase: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise
notes.note: The quotation is Isaiah 29:14, in a form close to the ancient Greek translation. In Isaiah the words are God’s judgment on the political advisers of Judah who trusted their own shrewdness.

In Jewish settings this word means a trained expert in the Scriptures and the Law, not a copyist, which is what ‘scribe’ suggests in English today. Most interpreters think Paul is setting the Jewish expert beside the Greek sage and the public debater, with echoes of Isaiah 19:12 and 33:18. In a Greek city the same word could also mean a civic secretary, but that sense is unlikely here.

The Greek word means ‘nations’ or ‘peoples’, and in the plural was the standard Jewish term for all peoples other than Israel; English versions render the one word as ‘Gentiles’ or ‘nations’ according to context. Here Paul uses it interchangeably with ‘Greeks’ in verses 22 and 24.

‘All flesh’ is a Hebrew way of saying ‘every human being’, with an overtone of human frailty before God; the idiom is kept here. The same Greek word lies behind ‘by human standards’ in verse 26, which is literally ‘according to the flesh’, so Paul’s argument begins and ends with merely human measures of worth.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice, justify. The word covers being in the right, doing what is right, and God’s action to set things right. ‘Righteousness’ is kept because ‘justice’ would suggest punishment to many modern readers, though some scholars prefer ‘justice’.

notes.phrase: Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.
notes.note: This is a condensed form of Jeremiah 9:24 (9:23 in the Greek version), not a word-for-word citation; the surrounding verses in Jeremiah warn the wise, the strong and the rich not to boast, which matches verses 26 to 28 here. In Jeremiah ‘the Lord’ is Israel’s God. Whether Paul means God or Christ by ‘the Lord’ here is debated.

candidates.rendering: flesh (v. 29); ‘by human standards’ for κατὰ σάρκα (v. 26)
candidates.reason: Paul’s uses range from the physical body to humanity to the sphere opposed to the Spirit, and translations vary widely between ‘flesh’, ‘human’, ‘sinful nature’ and ‘worldly’; readers need a consistent policy.
The plural address to mixed communities recurs in every letter and translations split between ‘brothers’, ‘brothers and sisters’ and ‘friends’.
Traditional ‘fellowship’ now misleads, and the word recurs in Acts, Paul and 1 John, where ‘partnership’, ‘sharing’, ‘participation’ and ‘communion’ all compete.
‘Scribe’ suggests a copyist to modern readers; the word is very frequent in the Gospels and needs one rendering (scholar, legal expert, teacher of the law) across the New Testament.
The verb and its noun recur throughout the New Testament and the choice between ‘gospel’ and ‘good news’, and between ‘preach’ and ‘proclaim’, should be made once.
